newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Investors put new faith in Africa.
newsitem.headline: Investors put new faith in Africa.

text.p: Foreigners are beginning to invest in Africa's services and manufacturing sectors in a shift away from the traditional commodities trade while the volume of U.S. investments is on the rise, a report said on Tuesday.

Although Africa missed the emerging markets boom of recent years, East Asia's tiger economies were becoming new players while U.S. firms were expanding their market share in a region where France has traditionally been the leading investor.

The 462-page report on 53 African countries by UNCTAD, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, said foreign direct investment in Africa remained low with total inflows of $5 billion in 1996, up from $3 billion a year in the late 1980s.

In the five years to 1995, Africa accounted for just five percent of foreign direct investment in the world's developing economies -- way below the regional share of eastern Europe but higher than former Soviet Central Asia's one percent.
But that could be changing thanks to liberalisation and reform policies which have produced favourable investment climates in a number of African countries, the report said.
The impoverished Africa, the former "Dark Continent" where wars and famines and bloodshed have raged for years, now has stock exchanges, Treasury bills and interbank markets.
The continent is a pot of mineral wealth and potentially a huge market where reformed countries will eventually become buyers of Western products.

Western Europe led by France and Britain continued to dominate Africa's foreign investment scene, the report said, but noted a dramatic rise in investments from the United States, now accounting for 20 percent of inflows from the developed world.

France by far remained the single biggest investor in Africa, accounting for 20 percent of total direct investments, 17 percent of capital investments in finance and insurance and more than a third of all foreign affiliates, the report said.

But the United States, which has begun courting reforming African countries in a new policy, increased its overseas direct investments in Africa to $1.2 billion in 1996 from $970 million in 1995 and only $173 million in 1994, UNCTAD figures showed.
More than 30 percent of U.S. flows went to South Africa, followed by Nigeria and Egypt.

With France in disarray over how to keep its exclusive control over Francophone Africa and Britain showing little interest in its former colonies, analysts say Washington appears well placed to fill in Africa's new power vacuum.
Overseas direct investment remained concentrated in a handful of countries, mainly oil-exporting. Nigeria and Egypt accounted for half, followed by Morocco and Angola.

UNCTAD said African firms led by South Africans and Nigerians were emerging as outward investors, venturing mostly into neighbouring countries in sectors ranging from tourism and satellite television to banking and retailing.
It noted that foreign direct investments in Africa were no longer concentrated in the traditional area of commodities.
Services including banking and insurance now accounted for the largest share of foreign direct investment in countries led by Egypt and South Africa, followed by manufacturing, it said.
Foreign direct investment now accounted for 10 percent of Gross Domestic Product of Africa, said the report.
UNCTAD noted growing interest in Africa by Southeast Asian countries led by Malaysia, which has been pushing for closer ties with South Africa, Ghana, Guinea and Zimbabwe and Namibia.
Its data also showed that African money once kept abroad was now slowly being invested in the continent.
--- Reuters Geneva Newsroom 41-22-733 38 31
